subject: math

unit.title: Calculation: add, subtract, multiply, divide
unit.essentialQuestion: How do we add and take away bigger numbers, and what does 'lots of' mean?

title: Adding two-digit numbers (with regrouping)
objectives: By the end, I can add two-digit numbers, exchanging ten ones for a ten when needed.

vocabulary.definition: put amounts together to find how much altogether
swap ten ones for one ten
move the traded ten over to the tens column

emphasize: When the ones make TEN OR MORE, you must exchange — ten ones become one ten. You can't keep 13 in the ones column.
Pre-empt the '713' error: writing 7 tens and 13 ones side by side (45 + 38 = '713').
Repeat the anchor phrase: 'Ten ones become one ten — trade them in.'

keyConcepts: regrouping/exchanging ten ones for a ten
misconceptions: 45 + 38 = '713' — writing 13 straight into the ones column with no exchange
always exchanging, even when the ones stay under ten
hooks: Two prices in a shop — 36p and 27p — how much altogether?

digital: virtual rods and cubes on the whiteboard block (animated exchange)

video.watchTask: Every time Mr. J trades ten ones for a ten, shout 'EXCHANGE!' — and watch where the new ten goes.

afterCheck.question: When did Mr. J have to exchange?
afterCheck.expectedAnswer: When the ones added up to ten or more.

plan.goal: Set the shop problem (36p + 27p) and tease 'the great exchange'; retrieve partitioning.
plan.note: Don't solve it yet — the exchange is the reveal of the explain beat.
plan.successCriteria: Child wants both toys and answers '30 and 6' for partitioning 36.

script.say: We're in the toy shop! A toy car costs 36p and a sticker pack costs 27p — and I want BOTH. How much do I need altogether? We'll build it with blocks… and somewhere in the middle we'll have to make a clever swap called the great exchange. Quick warm-up first: partition 36 — tens and ones?
script.adaptHints: Swap the car and stickers for two things the child would buy. Listen for '30 and 6'; if shaky, rebuild 36 as rods and count the tens.

stuckProtocol: If partitioning is shaky: draw 36 as 3 sticks and 6 dots and count the sticks in tens: 10, 20, 30.

plan.goal: Model 36 + 27 with virtual blocks: ones first (6 + 7 = 13), exchange ten ones for a ten, then total the tens.
plan.note: The animated whiteboard acts out the exchange — this is the concrete/pictorial heart of the lesson. Go slowly at the trade.
plan.successCriteria: Child sees the 13 ones become 1 ten + 3 ones and hears 'ten ones become one ten — trade them in'.

script.say: Watch me build it. 36 is 3 tens and 6 ones. Below it, 27 — 2 tens and 7 ones. Rule one: add the ONES first. 6 and 7 make 13 ones. But wait — I can't keep 13 ones in the ones column! It's too crowded. So here comes the great exchange: ten of those ones melt together into one shiny new ten-rod, and 3 ones stay behind. Now the tens: 30, plus 20, plus my brand-new 10 — that's 60. And the 3 ones left over. 60 and 3… 63! The car AND the stickers cost 63p.
script.adaptHints: Make the exchange moment dramatic — it's the whole lesson. Repeat: 'Ten ones become one ten — trade them in.'

elements.value: Ten ones become one ten — trade them in!

plan.goal: Shared build of 27 + 46: the child drives the exchange and states the final tens and ones.
plan.note: The character builds; the child decides each step. 7 + 6 = 13 → exchange → 7 tens and 3 ones = 73.
plan.successCriteria: Child says the ones make 13, calls for the exchange, and answers '7 tens and 3 ones — 73'.

script.say: Your turn to be the shopkeeper! Together: 27 + 46. I've built both numbers. Add the ones for me — 7 and 6 make…? … Thirteen! Can we keep 13 ones in the ones column? … No! Shout it with me: EXCHANGE! Ten ones become one ten. Now count it all up: after the swap, how many tens and how many ones?
script.adaptHints: Pause for the child at each decision. If they say '6 tens', ask: 'Don't forget the brand-new ten from the trade — now how many?'

blocks.text: 27 + 46: the ones make 13. After the trade there are ___ tens and 3 ones.

wrongAnswers.why: wrote the 13 ones straight into the answer — no exchange
wrongAnswers.remedy: Can 13 ones live in the ones column? Trade ten of them for a ten-rod — now count the tens again.

wrongAnswers.why: exchanged but forgot to add the carried ten
wrongAnswers.remedy: Where did your traded-in ten go? It has to join the tens: 20 + 40 + 10 = ?

plan.note: This is the KB misconception check. Watch the answer shape: '713' = no exchange; '73' = dropped the carried ten.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 83 and can show where the exchange happened.

script.say: Solo challenge! 45 + 38. Build it in your head or on the board — ones first, and watch out: this one needs the great exchange. Type your total.
script.adaptHints: After a correct answer, probe: 'Did you have to exchange? Show me the swap.'

wrongAnswers.why: wrote 7 tens and 13 ones side by side — no exchange
wrongAnswers.remedy: You can't keep 13 in the ones column. Swap ten ones for one ten — now how many tens do you have?

wrongAnswers.why: added the ones but dropped the traded ten
wrongAnswers.remedy: Where did your traded-in ten go? Add it to the tens column: 40 + 30 + 10 = ?

plan.goal: Independent adding with and WITHOUT exchange, so the child decides whether to trade; stretch to three numbers.
plan.note: Director draws from practiceBank, start level 2. Interleave a no-exchange sum (42 + 35) so trading is a decision, not a habit.
plan.successCriteria: Child solves 3+ additions correctly, including one with no exchange, explaining each time whether a trade was needed.

script.say: Shopkeeper practice! I'll give you sums — some need the great exchange, some don't. Your first job every time: add the ones and ask, 'is it ten or more?'
script.adaptHints: Frame sums as prices of things the child loves. Never change the numbers.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'I think the ten didn't get traded.'
Go fully concrete — act out the exchange slowly on the whiteboard, ten ones melting into one rod.
One hint: 'Count the ones — is it ten or more?'
Re-ask with smaller ones (43 + 24, no exchange needed), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child states when the exchange happens; end on an earned success.
plan.successCriteria: Child says the exchange happens 'when the ones make ten or more'.

script.say: Last question, shopkeeper: tell me — WHEN do we have to do the great exchange? … Exactly: when the ones make ten or more. You spotted exactly when to trade ten ones for a ten today — that's the whole secret of adding big numbers. Every giant sum you'll ever meet uses YOUR trick.
script.adaptHints: Praise the specific process observed: adding ones first, checking 'ten or more?', remembering the carried ten.

block.prompt: First step of 36 + 27: add the ones. 6 + 7 = ?

wrongAnswers.why: a bonds slip
wrongAnswers.remedy: Use the make-ten trick: 6 + 7 — take 4 from the 7 to fill the 6 up to ten. What's left?

wrongAnswers.why: wrote the digits side by side instead of adding
wrongAnswers.remedy: We're joining the cubes, not lining up digits. Count on from 6: seven more.

hints: Make ten first: 6 + 4 = 10, then add what's left of the 7.
Count on from 6: 7, 8, 9…

reteach.say: Ones first, always. Six cubes, then seven more: 6… 10 (that used 4 of them)… and 3 more makes 13. Six plus seven is thirteen — more than ten, so a trade is coming!

block.caption: 6 + 7 = 13 ones — too many for the ones column!

block.prompt: You added the ones and got 13. What do you do now?
options: Trade ten ones for one ten — 3 ones stay
Keep all 13 ones in the ones column
block.explain: Ten ones become one ten — trade them in. The new ten joins the tens column; 3 ones stay behind.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Trade ten ones for one ten — 3 ones stay

wrongAnswers.answer: Keep all 13 ones in the ones column
wrongAnswers.why: the no-exchange error — this is what creates answers like '713'
wrongAnswers.remedy: The ones column only holds up to 9. What can ten of those ones become?

wrongAnswers.why: thinks the leftover ones disappear
wrongAnswers.remedy: Nothing vanishes in maths! Ten ones trade in; the other 3 still count. Where do they live?

hints: Ten ones are worth exactly one…?
The ones column can never hold more than 9.

reteach.say: Think of it like a piggy-bank rule: ten pennies trade in for one shiny ten-coin. 13 ones → trade ten of them → one new ten, and 3 pennies stay. Nothing lost, just swapped!

block.title: The great exchange
steps: Ten ones become 1 ten; 3 ones stay
The new ten joins the tens column

wrongAnswers.why: kept 13 in the ones column — no exchange
wrongAnswers.remedy: 13 ones can't stay. Trade ten for a ten-rod — now count your tens: 20 + 40 + 10.

wrongAnswers.why: dropped the carried ten
wrongAnswers.remedy: Where did the traded ten go? It must join the tens: 20 + 40 + 10 = ?

hints: Ones first: 7 + 6 = ? Is it ten or more?
After the trade: how many tens altogether?

reteach.say: Slow motion: 27 is 2 tens 7 ones; 46 is 4 tens 6 ones. Ones: 7 + 6 = 13 → trade! One new ten, 3 ones stay. Tens: 20 + 40 + 10 = 70. Answer: 73.

wrongAnswers.why: kept 15 in the ones column — no exchange
wrongAnswers.remedy: 8 + 7 = 15 ones — too many! Trade ten of them. Now how many tens and ones?

wrongAnswers.why: dropped the carried ten
wrongAnswers.remedy: You traded ten ones for a new ten — did it join the tens? 40 + 30 + 10 = ?

hints: Ones first: 8 + 7 = ?
15 ones means a trade: 1 new ten and 5 ones stay.

reteach.say: Ones: 8 + 7 = 15 — ten or more, so trade! One new ten, 5 ones stay. Tens: 40 + 30 + 10 = 80. Total: 85.

wrongAnswers.why: kept 14 in the ones column — no exchange
wrongAnswers.remedy: 9 + 5 = 14 ones. Trade ten of them in — what's left in the ones, and how many tens now?

wrongAnswers.why: dropped the carried ten
wrongAnswers.remedy: The traded ten is missing! 20 + 20 + 10 = ?

hints: Ones first: 9 + 5 = ?
After trading: 4 ones stay, and the tens grow by one.

reteach.say: 9 + 5 = 14 ones → trade ten → 1 new ten, 4 ones stay. Tens: 20 + 20 + 10 = 50. So 29 + 25 = 54. The trade is what keeps the columns tidy.

block.explain: Check the ones: 2 + 5 = 7 — under ten, so no trade needed. 42 + 35 = 77, no exchange.

wrongAnswers.why: thinks every two-digit sum needs a trade
wrongAnswers.remedy: The trade only happens when the ones make ten or MORE. Add the ones: 2 + 5 = ? Is that ten or more?

wrongAnswers.answer: True, because the numbers are big
wrongAnswers.why: judging by the size of the numbers, not the ones
wrongAnswers.remedy: Big tens don't matter — only the ones decide. Look just at 2 + 5.

hints: Only the ones decide: 2 + 5 = ?
Trade only when the ones reach ten.

reteach.say: The exchange isn't for every sum — it's only for crowded ones columns. 2 + 5 = 7 ones: they all fit, no trade. Compare with 6 + 7 = 13: too crowded, trade! Always ask the ones first.

block.prompt: Match each sum to its total.

wrongAnswers.why: guessed by nearness instead of working the ones
wrongAnswers.remedy: Work it properly: 5 + 8 = 13 → trade → tens: 40 + 30 + 10. Which total matches?

wrongAnswers.why: swapped two answers — no self-check
wrongAnswers.remedy: Check one: 36 + 27 — ones make 13, trade, tens make 60. Which total has 3 ones?

hints: Work out the ones of each sum first — the ones digit of the total must match.
Only one sum here needs NO trade: find it first.

reteach.say: Match like a detective, using the ones. 36 + 27: ones 6 + 7 = 13, so the total ends in 3 → 63. 42 + 35: ones 2 + 5 = 7, ends in 7 → 77. The ones digit is your fingerprint!

wrongAnswers.why: missed one of the tens when totalling
wrongAnswers.remedy: Count the tens carefully: 10 + 20 + 10 = ? Then the ones: 2 + 3 + 4.

wrongAnswers.why: a ones slip while adding three numbers
wrongAnswers.remedy: Add the ones in pairs: 2 + 3 = 5, then 5 + 4 = ?

hints: Same plan: ALL the ones first (2 + 3 + 4), then all the tens.
Do the ones make ten or more? Then no trade needed here.

reteach.say: Three numbers, same trick. Ones: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 — under ten, no trade. Tens: 10 + 20 + 10 = 40. Total 49. However many numbers you add, it's always ones first, then tens.

wrongAnswers.why: dropped the ten inside 13
wrongAnswers.remedy: The ones made 6 + 7 — that's more than 3! Add them again: 6 + 7 = ?

wrongAnswers.why: kept the trade but lost the 3 leftover ones
wrongAnswers.remedy: Ten of the ones traded in, but 3 more are still there. 6 + 7 makes exactly…?

hints: The 50 is the tens: 30 + 20. What did the ones make?
6 + 7 = ? That whole amount goes in the gap.

reteach.say: This is the smash-and-add way: partition both numbers. Tens: 30 + 20 = 50. Ones: 6 + 7 = 13. Then 50 + 13 = 63 — the 13 carries its own ten across. Same answer as the blocks, written the fast way!

block.prompt: Sam says 45 + 38 = 713. Explain what went wrong, and give the real answer.
block.sample: Sam kept 13 in the ones column instead of trading. Ten ones become one ten: tens are 40 + 30 + 10 = 80, plus 3 ones — the real answer is 83.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Sam didn't exchange — 13 ones must become 1 ten and 3 ones; the real answer is 83

wrongAnswers.why: doesn't see the missing exchange
wrongAnswers.remedy: Look at Sam's 13 sitting in the ones. Can a column hold 13? What should ten of those ones become?

wrongAnswers.why: spotted the error but dropped the carried ten
wrongAnswers.remedy: Good — the 13 traded in! But the new ten must JOIN the tens: 40 + 30 + 10 = ?

hints: Where did Sam's 13 come from — and where should ten of it go?
Is 713 even a sensible size for 45 + 38? Estimate: about 50 + 40.

reteach.say: Sam's answer fails the size test: 45 + 38 is about 50 + 40 — around 90, nowhere near seven hundred! The 13 ones needed the great exchange: one new ten joins 40 + 30 to make 80, and 3 ones stay. 83.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → move up one level; at level 3, interleave exchange, no-exchange and three-number sums.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run that item's reteach with the exchange acted out slowly on the whiteboard, then serve a level-1 item (ones-only or 'what do you do with 13?').
adaptivity.masterySignal: 3+ correct across levels 2–3 including one sum WITH exchange, one WITHOUT (42 + 35 style), and the child stating when a trade is needed → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'two-digit addition with regrouping'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: 'the ten didn't get traded.'
Go fully concrete — act out the exchange slowly: ten ones melting into one rod.
One hint: 'Count the ones — is it ten or more?'
Re-ask with smaller ones (43 + 24, no exchange), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Frame every sum as prices or points from LearnerModel.interests (toy prices, match scores, sticker counts) — never change the numbers or the exchange language.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish with a sum the child can win (no-exchange if needed), then specific process praise: what they DID (added ones first, checked 'ten or more?', remembered the carried ten) — never 'you're so clever'.

differentiation.support: Act out the swap of 10 ones for 1 ten every single time so 45 + 38 can never become '713'; keep sums with one clear exchange; say 'ten ones become one ten' together at the trade.
differentiation.stretch: Add three two-digit numbers (12 + 23 + 14); estimate the total first, then check; invent two prices that need an exchange and two that don't.

extension: 'The great exchange' shop challenge — invent two prices that total exactly 80p (one pair must need an exchange, one pair must not), and prove each total with blocks.
assessmentEvidence: Child solves 2 two-digit additions with regrouping and one without, exchanging correctly, keeping the carried ten, and recording the right totals.
revisitLater: A two-digit addition with exchange as a starter in Lessons 8 and 12; the exchange idea reverses in Lesson 7 (breaking a ten) and returns with money in Lesson 16.
